title: What the Midterms Could Mean for Markets, Debt and AI Stocks
excerpt: Investors expect divided government, which history says stocks like — but a $40 trillion debt load and a 2027 debt-limit deadline make this cycle different.
body:
• Wall Street's base case for the November 3 midterms is divided government: forecasters expect Democrats to win the House, with the Senate less clear.
  • History favours stocks after midterms — Edward Jones data shows the S&P 500 rose an average of 1.7% in the month after the last 14 midterms and 15.5% over six months.
  • The debt is the pressure point: US debt has passed $40 trillion, and the Bipartisan Policy Center estimates the debt limit will be reached between late winter and midsummer 2027.
  • A Democratic sweep would raise oversight of AI spending; a Republican sweep would keep deregulation but likely widen deficits, analysts say.

As Americans vote in the midterm elections on Tuesday, investors are less worried about who wins than about what the result does to three things: federal spending, the national debt, and the AI boom that has carried the stock market.

Since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in 2025 with full Republican control of Congress, the S&P 500 has gained about 27%, powered by vast capital spending on artificial intelligence and strong earnings growth, according to Reuters. Treasury yields, however, are substantially higher, and current forecasts point to Democrats winning the House while control of the Senate remains less clear.

Why gridlock usually calms markets

Political gridlock has historically been good for markets because it limits Congress's ability to pass sweeping tax and spending legislation, reducing policy risk. Data from Edward Jones shows the S&P 500 rose an average of 1.7% in the month after the last 14 midterm elections dating back to 1970, and returned an average of 15.5% in the six months following them.

"Volatility around the vote is possible, but markets have historically performed well in the year following midterms as political uncertainty recedes and attention returns to the economic outlook."

— Magdalena Ocampo, Market Strategist, Principal Asset Management

"Less change makes a more predictable environment, which allows companies to invest in longer-term projects," Chris Low, chief economist at FHN Financial, said. "That tends to be good for earnings." UBS's chief investment office similarly assigns a 50% probability to a Democratic sweep, 40% to split control and 10% to Republicans holding both chambers — and advises investors not to treat the midterms as a binary event for equities, bonds or the dollar.

The debt-ceiling risk

The exception to the gridlock-is-good story is the debt. US national debt recently surpassed $40 trillion, and a divided Congress raises the risk of government shutdowns and debt-limit brinkmanship. The Bipartisan Policy Center estimates the US will reach the debt limit again sometime between late winter and midsummer 2027.

"Prolonged shutdowns and fiscal standoffs could push Treasury yields higher, weighing on equity valuations."

— Ed Yardeni, President, Yardeni Research

Yardeni also warned that a Democratic sweep could deliver a "cold shower" for stocks in the short term, though he said he would view a significant selloff as a buying opportunity given the strength of the economy and corporate earnings.

The AI angle

The biggest market effect of a strong Democratic showing could fall on the AI trade. If Democrats win both chambers, investors expect tougher oversight of artificial intelligence, with the power to investigate Corporate America and slow deregulation. Congressional probes could speed up efforts to require safety standards for frontier AI models and hold data center developers more accountable, Raymond James policy analyst Ed Mills noted. A Republican sweep runs the other way: low risk of new AI regulation, but scope for more tax reform and defense spending that would worsen an already large deficit.

What to watch

Results will arrive state by state through Tuesday night and Wednesday. For investors, the first signals will be in Treasury yields and the dollar on Wednesday morning, then in how the new Congress handles its first funding deadlines in early 2027. The historical pattern says the market's midterm hangover is usually short; the fiscal calendar says this cycle's argument is only beginning.
